newsitem.title: UK: UK's Rifkind sticks with word "hostile" over EMU.
newsitem.headline: UK's Rifkind sticks with word "hostile" over EMU.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said on Wednesday he did not regret using the word "hostile" to describe the government's attitude to a single European currency. "No I don't regret it because, in the context in which I was using it, it made sense and it was consistent with what the government's policy is," Rifkind told BBC radio. "What I and the chancellor and the prime minister all emphasise is that we are against joining a single currency in January 1999 because on all the evidence that is available at the moment that looks as if it would be on a fudged basis."
Earlier on Wednesday, Rifkind said the government was, on balance, hostile to a single currency.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said Rifkind was not trying to alter the government's wait-and-see approach to European economic and monetary union. It was "a slip of the tongue," he said.

Prime Minister John Major told reporters: "We would need to be persuaded that it (EMU) was better. We are not so persuaded at the moment and we think it is very unlikely that the circumstances will be right by January 1, 1999, not just for us but right the way across Europe."
But he stressed that the government's "wait and see" policy remained in place.
